readings.c1s2:
< OF. *''wardour'', ''gardour'', ''gardeor'', a keeper, warder, < ''warder'', ward: see ''ward''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'', and ''-er''<sup>1</sup>, ''-or''<sup>1</sup>.] One who keeps watch and ward; a keeper; a guard.
{{smaller block|Memory, the ''warder'' of the brain.
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, i. 7. 65.}}
The ''warders'' of the gate.
{{right|''Dryden'', Æneid, ii. 451.}}}}

'''Warder butcher-bird†''', {{smaller|the great gray shrike, ''Lanius excubitor. Sir John Sebright.''}}

'''warder<sup>2</sup>''' (wâr′dėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''warder'', ''wardrere'', ''wardere­re''; appar. < ''ward''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'', + ''-er''<sup>2</sup>.] A truncheon or staff of authority carried by a king, commander-in-chief, or other important dignitary. {{smaller|Signals seem to have been given by means of it, as by casting it down (a signal to stop proceedings) or throwing it up (a signal to charge).}}
{{smaller block|Stay, the king hath thrown his ''warder'' down.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., i. 3. 118.}}
<poem>Wafting his ''warder'' thrice about his head,
[He] cast it up with his auspicious hand,
Which was the signal through the English spread
That they should charge.</poem>
{{right|''Drayton'', Battle of Agincourt, st. 181.}}}}

'''warderere†'''. A doubtful word occurring only in the following passage describing the pursuit of a horse that had run away.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thise sely clerkes rennen up and doun
With “Keepe! Keepe! stand! stand! Jossa ''warderere!''”
[var. ''ware the rere'', Camb. MS., ''warederere'', Harl. MS., ''warth there'', 16th cent. ed.]</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Reeve’s Tale, l. 181.}}}}

'''ward-holding''' (wârd′hōl″ding), ''n.'' The ancient military tenure in Scotland, by which vassals were at first obliged to serve the superior in war as often as his occasions called for it.

'''Wardian''' (wâr′di-an), ''a.'' [< ''Ward'' (see def.)
readings.c1s3:
+ ''-ian''.] Invented by, or otherwise relating to, a person named Ward.—{{smaller|'''Wardian case''', a portable inclosure with a wooden base and glass sides and top, invented by Nathaniel B. Ward, an Englishman, and serving for the transportation of delicate living plants, or for their maintenance as an indoor ornament. The base is lined with zinc, or supplied with an earthen tray. The confined air preserves its moisture, and ferns, mosses, and other shade-loving plants develop in it with great beauty.}}

'''warding-file''' (wâr′ding-fīl), ''n.'' A flat file of uniform thickness, cut only at the edges: used to file the ward-notches in keys. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''wardless''' (wârd′les), ''a.'' [< ''ward''<sup>1</sup> + ''-less.''] That cannot be warded off or avoided. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|He gives like destiny a ''wardless'' blow.
{{right|''Stephen Harvey'', tr. of Juvenal’s Satires, ix. 174.}}}}

'''wardman†''' (wârd′man), ''n.'' [< ''ward''<sup>2</sup> + ''man.''] A town officer in England.
{{smaller block|The common ''wardman'' . . . carries the largest of the silver maces and in processions immediately precedes the mayor. {{right|''Jewitt'', Art Journal, 1881, p. 105.}}}}

'''ward-mote''' (wârd′mōt), ''n.'' A meeting of a ward; also, a court formerly held in every ward in the city of London. Also called ''wardmote-court'' or ''inquest.''

'''wardone†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''warden''<sup>2</sup>.

'''wardour†''', ''n.'' An old spelling of ''warder''<sup>1</sup>.

'''ward-penny''' (wârd′pen″i), ''n.'' Same as ''wardage.''

'''wardrobe''' (wârd′rōb), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''wardrope, wardroppe''; < ME. ''warderobe, wardrope, wardedrope'', < OF. ''warderobe, garderobe, garderobbe'', a wardrobe, also a privy, < ''warder'', ward,

{{RunningHeader|warden|6822|ware}}see ''warden''1. But the sense of ''warden'' is active, ‘one who keeps,’ and it does not seem to apply to a pear; and the ME. forms of ''warden''1 are different from those of ''warden''2. Perhaps the origin is in OF. *''wardon'', a var. of ''gardon'' (Godefroy), a var. of ''gardin'', garden: see ''garden''.] A kind of pear, used chiefly for roasting or baking. {{smaller block|''Wardone'', peere, volemum. ''Wardone'' tree, volemus. {{right|''Prompt. Parv.'', p. 516.}}}} {{smaller block|Faith, I would have had him roasted like a ''warden'', In brown paper, and no more talk on ’t. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Cupid’s Revenge, ii. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|Ox-cheek when hot, and ''wardens'' bak’d, some cry; But ’tis with an intention men should buy. {{right|''W. King'', Art of Cookery, l. 541.}}}} '''Warden pie''', a pie made of warden pears, baked or stewed without crust. {{smaller block|I must have saffron to colour the ''warden pies''. {{right|''Shak.'', W. T., iv. 3. 48.}}}} '''wardenry''' (wâr′dn-ri), ''n.''   [< ''warden''1 + ''-ry'' (see ''-ery'').]   '''1.''' The district in charge of a warden. {{smaller block|But yet they may not tamely see, All through the Western ''Wardenry'', Your law-contemning kinsmen ride, And burn and spoil the Border-side. {{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., iv. 24.}}}} '''2.''' The office of warden. '''wardenship''' (wâr′dn-ship), ''n.''   [< ''warden''1 + ''-ship''.]   The office of warden. {{smaller block|His Maj. K. Cha. I. gave him the ''Wardenship'' of Merton Colledge as a reward for his service, but the times suffered him not to receive or enjoy any benefitt by it. {{right|''Aubrey'', Lives (William Harvey).}}}} '''warder'''1 (wâr′dėr), ''n.''   [Formerly also ''wardour'', < OF. *''wardour'', ''gardour'', ''gardeor'', a keeper, warder, < ''warder'', ward: see ''ward''1, ''v.'', and ''-er''1, ''-or''1.]   One who keeps watch and ward; a keeper; a guard. {{smaller block|Memory, the ''warder'' of the brain. {{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, i. 7. 65.}}}} {{smaller block|The ''warders'' of the gate. {{right|''Dryden'', Æneid, ii. 451.}}}} '''Warder butcher-bird†''', {{smaller|the great gray shrike, ''Lanius excubitor. Sir John Sebright.''}} '''warder2''' (wâr′dėr), ''n.''   [< ME. MS., ''warth there'', 16th cent. ed.] {{right|''Chaucer'', Reeve’s Tale, l. 181.}}}} '''ward-holding''' (wârd′hōl″ding), ''n.'' The ancient military tenure in Scotland, by which vassals were at first obliged to serve the superior in war as often as his occasions called for it. '''Wardian''' (wâr′di-an), ''a.''   [< ''Ward'' (see def.) + ''-ian''.]   Invented by, or otherwise relating to, a person named Ward.—{{smaller|'''Wardian case''', a portable inclosure with a wooden base and glass sides and top, invented by Nathaniel B. Ward, an Englishman, and serving for the transportation of delicate living plants, or for their maintenance as an indoor ornament. The base is lined with zinc, or supplied with an earthen tray. The confined air preserves its moisture, and ferns, mosses, and other shade-loving plants develop in it with great beauty.}} '''warding-file''' (wâr′ding-fīl), ''n.'' A meeting of a ward; also, a court formerly held in every ward in the city of London. Also called ''wardmote-court'' or ''inquest.'' '''wardone†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''warden''2. '''wardour†''', ''n.'' An old spelling of ''warder''1. '''ward-penny''' (wârd′pen″i), ''n.'' Same as ''wardage.'' '''wardrobe''' (wârd′rōb), ''n.''   [Formerly also ''wardrope, wardroppe''; < ME. ''warderobe, wardrope, wardedrope'', < OF. ''warderobe, garderobe, garderobbe'', a wardrobe, also a privy, < ''warder'', ward, keep, + ''robe'', ''robbe'', garment: see ''ward''1 and ''robe''1.]   '''1.''' Originally, a room or large closet in which clothes were kept, and in which the making of clothes, repairing, etc., were carried on. {{smaller block|But who that departed, Gyomar ne departed neuer, but a-bode spekynge with Morgain, the sustur of kynge Arthur, in a ''wardrope'' vnder the paleys, where she wrought with silke and golde. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 507.}}}} {{smaller block|The last day of Octobre, the . . . yere of the reyne of King Henri the Sixt, Sir John Fastolf, Knyght, hath lefte in his ''warde-drope'' at Castre this stuffe of clothys, and othir harnays that followith. {{right|''Paston Letters'', I. 475.}}}} {{smaller block|When first he spies His Prince’s ''Wardrobe'' ope, quite through is shot With wondring fear. ''J. Beaumont'', Psyche, iii. 75. God clothed us; . . . he hath opened his ''wardrobe'' unto us. {{right|''Donne'', Sermons, vii.}}}} '''2.''' A piece of furniture for the keeping of clothes, especially a large press closed by means of a door or doors, in which clothes can be hung up, and sometimes having shelves and drawers as well. {{smaller block|There! Carter has done with you, or nearly so; I’ll make you decent in a trice. Jane, . . . open the top drawer of the ''wardrobe'', and take out a clean shirt and neck-handkerchief: bring them here; and be nimble. {{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Jane Eyre, xx.}}}} {{smaller block|A ponderous mahogany ''wardrobe'', looking like nothing so much as a grim wooden mausoleum, occupied nearly all of one wall. {{right|''Harper’s Mag.'', LXXVI. 192.}}}} '''3.''' The clothes belonging to one person at one time. {{smaller block|''Hot.'' The king hath many marching in his coats. ''Doug.'' Now, by my sword, I will kill all his coats; I’ll murder all his ''wardrobe'', piece by piece. {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., v. 3. 27.}}}} {{smaller block|The most important article of all in a gentleman’s ''wardrobe'' was still wanting. {{right|''Barham'', Ingoldsby Legends, I. 14.}}}} '''4†.''' A privy. {{smaller block|I seye that in a ''wardrobe'' they him threwe. {{right|''Chaucer'', Prioress’s Tale, l. 120.}}}} '''wardrober''' (wârd′rō″bėr), ''n.''   [< ME. ''warderopere''; < ''wardrobe'' + ''-er''2.]   The keeper of a wardrobe. {{smaller block|An indenture . . . in which Peter Curteys, the king’s ''wardrober'', undertakes to furnish by the 3rd of July the articles specified for the coronation of King Richard. {{right|''J. Gairdner'', Richard III., iv.}}}} '''ward-room''' (wârd′röm), ''n.'' The apartment assigned to the commissioned officers of a man-of-war other than the commanding officer. Line-officers occupy staterooms on the starboard side and staff-officers on the port side.—'''Ward-room officers''', {{smaller|commissioned officers messing in the ward-room.}}—'''Ward-room steward.''' {{smaller|See ''steward'', 2 (''b'').}} '''wardrope†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''wardrobe''. '''Wardrop’s disease.''' A malignant form of inflammation occurring at the root, or on one side, of a nail. '''Wardrop’s operation for aneurism.''' See ''operation''. '''Ward’s electuary.''' A confection of black pepper. '''wardship1''' (wârd′ship), ''n.''   [< ''ward''1 + ''-ship''.]   The office of a ward or guardian; guardianship; care and protection of a ward; right of guardianship; hence, the feudal tenure by which the lord claimed the custody of the body and custody and profits of the lands of the infant heir of his deceased tenant. {{smaller block|And we . . . come in the court, and Bertylmeu havynge this termys to Bernard, seying, “Sir, forasmych as the Kyng hathe grauntyd be hese lettres patent the ''wardship'' with the profites of the londes of T. Fastolf duryng hese nun age to you and T. H., wherfor I am comyn as ther styward, be ther comaundement.” {{right|''Paston Letters'', I. 306.}}}} {{smaller block|Ecclesiastical persons were by ancient order forbidden to be executors of any man’s testament, or to undertake the ''wardship'' of children. {{right|''Hooker'', Eccles. Polity, vii. 15.}}}} Thou grand impostor! how hast thou obtained The ''wardship'' of the world?{{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, ii. 3.}} '''wardship2''' (wârd′ship), ''n.''   [< ''ward''2 + ''-ship''.]   The state or condition of a ward; pupilage. {{smaller block|In certain nations, women, whether married or not, have been placed in a state of perpetual ''wardship.'' {{right|''Bentham'', Introd. to Morals and Legislation, xvi. 44, note.}}}} '''wardsman''' (wârdz′man), ''n.''; pl. ''wardsmen'' (-men). One who keeps watch and ward; a guard.   ''Sydney Smith.'' [Rare.] '''Ward’s paste.''' Same as ''Ward’s electuary.'' '''wardstaff†''' (wârd′stȧf), ''n.'' Same as ''warder''2. '''wardwit''' (wârd′wit), ''n.'' The being quit of giving money for the keeping of ward in a town. '''ware1''' (wãr), ''a.''   [< ME. ''ware'', ''war'', < AS. ''wær'', also ''gewær'' (> E. ''aware''), watchful, heedful, cautious, = OS. ''war'', also ''giwar'' = D. ''gewaar'' = OHG. ''giwar'', MHG. ''gewar'', G. ''gewahr'', aware, = Icel. ''varr'' = Dan. Sw. ''var'' = Goth. ''wars'', watchful; from a Teut. √ ''war'', watch, take heed, = L. ''vereri'', regard, respect, esteem, dread (see ''revere''1), = Gr. ὁρᾶν, perceive, look out for, observe (> οὐρος, watchman, guard), = Skt. √ ''var'', cover, surround. From the same source are ult. ''aware'' (of which ''ware''1 in mod. use is prob. in part an aphetic form), ''ward''1, ''ward''2, ''guard'', ''regard'', ''reward'', etc., ''revere''1, etc. ''Ware'' preceded by ''be'' has become merged with it, ''beware'' (as ''gone'' with ''be'' in ''begone''): see ''beware''. Hence the later adj. ''wary''1.]   '''1†.''' Watchful; cautious; prudent; wary. {{smaller block|Of me the worthy was ''war'', & my wille knew. {{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 13235.}}}} {{smaller block|The Erle to truste was noo daunger in, ffor he was ''ware'' and wise, I yow ensure. {{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1084.}}}} {{smaller block|Howe ''ware'' and circumspecte they aught to be. {{right|''Sir T. Elyot'', The Governour, iii. 11.}}}} '''2.''' On guard; on the watch (against something). See ''beware''. {{smaller block|Reason he made right, But bid her well be ''ware'', and still erect; Lest, by some fair-appearing good surprised, She dictate false, and misinform the will. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., ix. 353.}}}} '''3.''' Aware; conscious; assured. [Archaic.] {{smaller block|Ful fetys was hir cloke, as I was ''war''. {{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T., l. 157.}}}} {{smaller block|And Geaunt reised his axe to recouer a-nothor stroke, but Arthur was ther-of ''ware'', and smote the horse with the spores and passed forth, and than returned with his swerde. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 223.}}}} {{smaller block|Then was I ''ware'' of one that on me moved In golden armor with a crown of gold. {{right|''Tennyson'', Holy Grail.}}}} '''ware1''' (wãr), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''wared'', ppr. ''waring''.   [< ME. ''waren'', ''warien'', ''ware'', < AS. ''warian'', be on one’s guard, heed, look out (= OFries. ''waria'' = OS. ''warōn'' = OHG. ''bewarōn'', heed, = Icel. ''vara'', heed; hence ult. OF. ''garer'' = Pr. ''garar'', ''guarar'', be on one’s guard, heed), < ''wær'', watchful, heedful: see ''ware''1, ''a.'' Cf. ''wear''2, ''v.'']   To take care of; take precautions against; take heed to; look out for and guard against; beware of: as, ''ware'' the dog. Except in a few phrases, as in ''ware'' hawk, ''ware'' hounds, ''beware'' is now used instead of ''ware''. {{smaller block|''Ware'' the sonne in his ascencioun
Ne fynde yow nat repleet of humours hote. {{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Nun’s Priest’s Tale, l. 136.}}}} {{smaller block|But ''warre'' the fox, as while thai sitte on brode
To sette in an Ilande were ful goode. {{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 23.}}}} '''ware2''' (wãr), ''n.''   [< ME. ''ware'', merchandise, goods, < AS. *''ware'', pl. ''waru'', wares (= D. ''waar'', a ware, commodity, pl. ''waren'', wares; cf. MD. ''waren'' = G. ''waare'', pl. ''waaren'' = Icel. ''vara'', pl. ''vörur'', wares, = Dan. ''vare'', pl. ''varer'' (cf. ''vare'', care), = Sw. ''vara'', pl. ''varor'', ware, wares); prob. akin to AS. ''waru'', guard, protection, care, custody, = G. ''wahre'' = Dan. ''vare'' = Sw. ''vara'', care; < Teut. √ ''war'', guard: see ''ware''1, ''a.'', and cf. ''worth''2.]   '''1.''' Articles of manufacture or merchandise: now usually in the plural. {{smaller block|No marchaunt yit ne fette outlandish ''ware''. {{right|''Chaucer'', Former Age, l. 22.}}}} {{smaller block|This is the ''ware'' wherein consists my wealth. {{right|''Marlowe'', Jew of Malta, i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|They shall not . . . sell or buy any maner of ''wares'', goods, or marchandises, secretely nor openly, by way of fraude, barat, or deceite.{{right|''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', I. 210.}}}} {{smaller block|You pretend buying of ''wares'' or selling of lands.{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, v. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|Who but a fool would have faith in a tradesman’s ''ware'' or his word?{{right|''Tennyson'', Maud, vii.}}}} '''2.''' A collective noun used generally in composition with the name of the material, or a term relating to the characters of the articles or the use to which they are put: as, ''china-ware'', ''tinware'', ''hardware'', ''tableware''.{{smaller|—'''Adams’s ware''', in ''ceram.'', a fine English pottery made at Tunstall, at the end of the eighteenth century, by William Adams, a pupil of Wedgwood. The pieces are often close imitations of the Wedgwood ware.—'''Agen ware.''' (''a'') An inferior kind of Roman pottery, softer and coarser than Samian ware: so called from Agen in the department of Lot-et-Garonne, France, where much of this ware was found with the furnaces. (''b'') A decorative pottery made in the seventeenth century, many of the pieces having the forms of animals.   ''Brongniart.''—'''Apulian ware.''' See ''Apulian pottery'' (under ''Apulian''), and cut under ''stamnos''.—'''Aretine ware.''' See ''Aretine''.—'''Awata ware,''' pottery and porcelain made at Awata, near Kioto, Japan. The greater number of the pieces known to be of this manufacture are of yellowish hard paste, with a crackled glaze as if in imitation of Satsuma ware; but a curious and beautiful imitation of old Delft and a thin porcelain of a peculiar grayish white are known.—'''Bamboo ware,''' a variety of Wedgwood ware: so named from its color, and otherwise known as ''cane-colored ware''.—'''Basalt ware.''' See ''basalt''.—'''Benares ware,''' a name given to a kind of ornamental metal-work made in India, in which a pattern is produced by chasing or in other ways depressing the surface of the metal.—'''Black ware.''' Same as ''basalt ware''.—'''Blue jasper ware,''' a name given to a blue-glazed pottery of modern manufacture, especially that made at the Ferrybridge factory.—'''Böttger ware.''' (''a'') A fine stoneware varying}}
